questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072133/assets/c800644be3cc0ad0688d52948a4a2cb813cbe14b1fe899abe5a1d92613a687bf.png)

Consider the picture above. Given that $r=\lambda p+\mu q$, find $\lambda $ and $\mu .$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072133/assets/90272fad8af526de6e169faba8daae29210c1f502c4959d0e1829e5ad65476f0.png)

In $△OPR$ shown above, we have 

- $OP=2|p|$

- $\overset{\to }{OP}$ and $p$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{OP}=2p.$

Similarly:

- $PR=4|q|$

- $\overset{\to }{PR}$ and $q$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PR}=4q.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PR} \\  & =2p+4q.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $r=\lambda p+\mu q=2p+4q.$

Since $p∦q,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

- $\lambda =2$ and $\mu =4$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072133/assets/c4d26b3db6446f586ca47634d9f9a3a004968a0081b8859ce46b4b4af799d066.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OH}=h,$ $\overset{\to }{OI}=i$ and $J$ divides $\overset{―}{HI}$ in the ratio $HJ:JI=3:7.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OJ}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OJ}=\overset{\to }{OH}+\overset{\to }{HJ}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OH}=h,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{HJ}.$

First, from $△OHI,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{HI} & =\overset{\to }{HO}+\overset{\to }{OI} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OH}+\overset{\to }{OI} \\  & =-h+i \\  & =i-h.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $HJ:JI=3:7,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{HJ}=\frac{3}{10}\overset{\to }{HI}=\frac{3}{10}(i-h).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OJ} & =\overset{\to }{OH}+\overset{\to }{HJ} \\  & =h+\frac{3}{10}(i-h) \\  & =\frac{7}{10}h+\frac{3}{10}i.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072133/assets/bae20e625c529ef2157faa4d534a19529c605c9002ed750e56723ff29e265226.png)

Consider the picture above. If $c=\lambda a-4b,$ then

$\lambda =$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a-4b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $-4b.$ So, we first draw the vector $-4b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072133/assets/139a4d4312ecbe42cd3a3859af4f4d7b93f8bbc54548ac5a0244c04e7ba5287b.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $-4b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=3|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=-3a.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =-4b-3a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a-4b=-3a-4b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =-3.
$$

- $\overset{\to }{XT}$ has the opposite direction to $k$

Additionally,

$$
t=\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XT}=-2j-\frac{1}{2}k.
$$

Consequently, $t=\lambda j+\mu k=-2j-\frac{1}{2}k.$

Since $k∦j,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

- $\lambda =-2$ and $\mu =-\frac{1}{2}$
